name: Kola
catalog_quote: It is not predictable whether stress occurs on the penultimate or the ultimate syllable of monomorphemic words. Penultimate stress, however, is most common in Kola. It should be noted that stress only falls on the root and never on affixes or clitics. In addition, stress does not occur beyond the penult of the root.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant: lexical penult-vs-ultima contrast within a root-final two-syllable window, penult dominant; Gordon 2002's plain 'Penult' flagged as over-coding) rests directly on the primary and only phonological description of Kola, Takata & Takata 1992 NUSA 34:40 sec. 2.5, which we hold as the full article PDF with page images; the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p. 40 and the p. 43 phonological-word statement is also there. The coding faithfully reflects the source ('not predictable whether... penultimate or ultimate... Penultimate stress, however, is most common... stress does not occur beyond the penult of the root'), so the contra note against Gordon 2002 is justified. Glottolog lists only three descriptive works; the one we lacked (de Winne 2013, 219-pp Leiden MA morphosyntax sketch) was fetched sources and is silent on stress beyond citing T&T 1992, and e

sources.citation: de Winne, David. 2013. A morphosyntax sketch of Kola, an Austronesian language of Aru, eastern Indonesia. MA thesis (Language Diversity), Universiteit Leiden, supervisor A. Schapper. 219 pp. Open Access, hdl.handle.net/1887/43445.
sources.quote: No independent stress analysis. States that Takata & Takata (1992) 'a phonology sketch, covers ... stress patterns ... and phonological word structure'; the thesis is based on the Takata et al. 1991 phrasebook with 'no access to any sound files of Kola'; 'More investigation into Kola's phonology is needed'; 'Currently there is no one actively working on Kola.' Reduplication rules are restated as targeting the stressed syllable, following T&T 1992:45.
sources.locator: pp. 3-4 (sec. 1.2.2-1.3) and 'Variation in Spelling' preface; reduplication sec. (Table 32, p. 124) cites T&T 1992:45 stressed-syllable rules
sources.note: Only post-1992 description of Kola in Glottolog; fetched sources to check for any newer stress statement. It has none and defers to Takata & Takata 1992, confirming that source as the state of the art.

sources.citation: Rehg, Kenneth L. 1993. Review of Burquest & Laidig (eds.) 1992, Descriptive Studies in Languages of Maluku (NUSA 34). Cakalele 4 (reviews section, together with van Engelenhoven's review of Phonological Studies in Four Languages of Maluku). ScholarSpace hdl 10125/4133.
sources.quote: Notes the paper 'provides descriptions of stress, syllable structure, and phoneme distribution'; criticises the vowel-height terminology and the definition of the phonological word as a 'stress group ... one of which receives a primary stress' (p. 43) as non-operational, and notes consonant coalescence is 'conditioned by place of articulation as well as by stress'. Does not dispute the penult/ultima lexical contrast or the penult-most-common statement.
